title: Planning the build
oneLiner: Before writing code, the agent reads what exists and makes a plan, like a recipe or a protocol.

analogy.office: A team meeting at the whiteboard before work starts.
analogy.lab: Writing your protocol before you touch a pipette.
analogy.kitchen: Reading the whole recipe before you turn on the stove.

title: What is a frontend?
oneLiner: The frontend is everything the user sees and clicks: pages, buttons, colors.

analogy.office: The shop window and the front desk.
analogy.lab: The microscope image you actually look at, not the machinery inside.
analogy.kitchen: The plated dish the guest sees on the table.

title: Components
oneLiner: Screens are built from small reusable pieces called components, like a button or a chart.

analogy.office: Standard forms you reuse instead of writing a new one each time.
analogy.lab: Reusable lab equipment: the same pipette works for every experiment.
analogy.kitchen: A sauce you make once and use on many dishes.

title: What is an API?
oneLiner: An API is a set of agreed requests one program can send another, and the answers it gets back.

analogy.office: The mail room: you send a request in the right format and get a reply.
analogy.lab: The sample intake window: drop off a labeled sample, get results back.
analogy.kitchen: The order window: a ticket goes in, a finished dish comes out.

title: What is a database?
oneLiner: A database stores information so it is still there tomorrow, organized so it can be found fast.

analogy.office: The archive with labeled filing cabinets.
analogy.lab: The freezer with sample boxes in a numbered grid.
analogy.kitchen: The pantry where every jar has its own shelf.

title: Schema
oneLiner: A schema is the plan for what each record holds, like the columns of a spreadsheet.

analogy.office: The template every form must follow.
analogy.lab: Your sample label format: ID, date, species, condition.
analogy.kitchen: The label on every container: what it is and when it was made.

title: Login and permissions
oneLiner: Authentication checks who you are; authorization decides what you are allowed to do.

analogy.office: The security desk checks your badge, and your badge opens only some doors.
analogy.lab: Badge access: anyone can enter the building, only trained people enter the BSL-2 room.
analogy.kitchen: Staff only: guests can order, only cooks go behind the line.

title: Why tests?
oneLiner: Tests are small automatic checks that the code still does what it should after every change.

analogy.office: Quality check before a product ships.
analogy.lab: Running a control alongside every experiment.
analogy.kitchen: Tasting the soup before it leaves the kitchen.

title: Dependencies
oneLiner: Dependencies are code other people wrote that the app uses, installed from a shared library.

analogy.office: Ordering supplies instead of making your own paper.
analogy.lab: Buying a reagent kit instead of synthesizing every chemical.
analogy.kitchen: Buying bread from a bakery instead of baking it yourself.

title: The terminal
oneLiner: The terminal is a text window where the agent types commands to run tools on your computer.

analogy.office: Giving instructions to an assistant by typing short notes.
analogy.lab: The control panel of an instrument.
analogy.kitchen: Calling out orders to the kitchen line.
